title: Rescuing an Existing Project
text: Trying to perfect an inherited project before understanding it can destroy useful context. Rescue begins with a safe inventory and a clear uncertainty record.

title: Rescuing an Existing Project
text:
Triage sequence

Freeze and preserve the current state; do not silently overwrite inputs or outputs.
Inventory files, scripts, data locations, access constraints, environments, and recent results.
Ask the previous owner or stakeholders what is trusted, provisional, or broken.
Reconstruct the smallest defensible path from an input to a named result.
Record gaps as risks and choose a stopping point for rescue work.
Create a handoff note before making major changes.







Important



Unlabeled cleanup can erase provenance. Keep a dated rescue log and preserve the original state when permissions and storage allow.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
Proposed draft policy — review required



This page proposes a minimum standard. It is not approved policy. Institutional, legal, contractual, privacy, security, records-management, funder, and data-governance requirements take precedence.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
1. Purpose
The minimum standard makes GeoEpi projects understandable, reviewable, reproducible where access permits, and transferable across people and time. A requirement belongs here only when failure materially threatens scientific defensibility, data security, result traceability, project continuity, collaboration, publication, operational use, handoff, or preservation.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
2. Scope
Apply this standard to active GeoEpi research, surveillance, field-data, software, modeling, simulation, operational, and HPC projects. Apply it proportionally to exploratory work and legacy projects. It covers project records and workflows, not scientific conclusions or a single software stack.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
3. Guiding principle
The GeoEpi Lab Book is a living resource. The minimum is a floor for defensibility and continuity, not a rigid template for every project. Use Required for universal controls, Conditionally required when project characteristics trigger a control, Recommended for practices that improve quality but are not universal, and Optional for useful local choices.
The required artifacts describe information that must be retained and discoverable. They do not necessarily require separate files. A README, configuration file, rendered report, workflow manifest, validated dataset, or automated log may satisfy multiple requirements when the information is clear, durable, and traceable. Separate formal records become necessary when project complexity, risk, contributors, operational importance, or institutional requirements justify them.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
4. Definitions

Source data: received or collected data preserved without undocumented modification.
Derived data: data created by a documented transformation from source or staged data.
Consequential: capable of changing a reported result, operational action, data protection, or project handoff.
Result traceability: the ability to identify inputs, code, parameters, environment, execution, and output for a result.
Authoritative location: the project location designated as current for a specified artifact or workflow.
Project artifact: a durable record needed to understand, execute, review, release, hand off, or close a project.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
5. Universal minimum requirements

Project identity — Required
Every active project must identify a stable title or identifier, project lead, primary analytical or data-management contact, research or operational objective, intended outputs, audience or decision context, current status, and authoritative repository or project location.
Every project must contain a concise scope statement identifying its objective, intended output, owner, authoritative location, and current status. For a small project, the README may contain this scope statement; a separate charter is not universal.


Project README — Required
Every active project must have a current project-level README covering purpose, responsible personnel, repository structure, data locations, setup requirements, principal workflows, expected outputs, access restrictions, current status, known limitations, and contact or handoff information. Use templates/project-readme-template.md.


Directory and object organization — Required
Separate source data, interim/staged data, derived data, analysis code, configuration, documentation, outputs, logs, and temporary files. Repository-specific names are permitted when their meanings are documented. No universal folder tree is required.


Source-data protection — Required
Preserve source data without undocumented modification. A correction must be reproducible, recorded, attributable, and linked to the corrected or derived version. Do not put protected source data in Git unless authorized.


Data provenance — Required
For each external or internally collected dataset, record a stable local identifier, source, collector/provider, acquisition method and date, original filename or source identifier, version/release date, license or use restriction, a checksum when proportionate, and transformations connecting source to derived data.
When the transformation chain is clear, versioned scripts and their retained outputs may constitute the source-to-derived provenance record; a separate provenance table is conditional.


Data classification and protection — Required
Identify relevant restrictions, such as public, internal, restricted, confidential, personally identifiable, proprietary, governed by a data-use agreement, or sensitive ecological/geographical information. These labels are descriptive until institutional terminology is approved; do not invent USDA or laboratory classification policy.


Metadata and data dictionaries — Required
Document variables, units, data types, identifiers, categories/codes, missing-value conventions, date/time conventions, coordinate reference systems, spatial units, temporal support, and important derivations. Use the data dictionary template where a table is appropriate.


Scripted transformations — Required
Retain consequential transformations and analyses in scripts, workflows, notebooks, or rendered computational documents. A manual step is permitted only when scripting is not reasonable, the procedure and inputs/outputs are documented, the responsible person is recorded, and the effect can be reviewed.


Version control — Required
Use Git-based version control for code and documentation unless a documented exception applies. Git is generally not the correct storage location for credentials, protected data, large raw datasets, sensitive spatial records, temporary files, generated caches, or non-redistributable proprietary material.


Software and computational environment — Required
Record enough environment information to reconstruct the project at a level proportional to risk and complexity. This may include R and package versions, renv.lock, a Python environment, containers, system libraries, external command-line tools, GIS/database versions, HPC modules, and operating-system details. renv is not universal.


Configuration and parameters — Required
Represent consequential paths and parameters explicitly through configuration files, command-line arguments, function arguments, workflow manifests, or documented constants. Major results must not depend solely on undocumented interactive state. A configuration file, workflow manifest, or documented function or command invocation may constitute the parameter record; a separate parameter document is not required when the information is already clear.


Quality assurance — Required
Document checks appropriate to the workflow. Examples include schema, missingness, duplicates, ranges, units, identifiers, temporal consistency, spatial validity, geometry, raster alignment, masks/exclusions, output completeness, model convergence, and simulation completion. Do not impose irrelevant checks. An executable QA script and retained report or log may constitute the QA/QC record when the checks, results, exceptions, and reviewer are discoverable.


Result traceability — Required
Every externally reported or operationally consequential result must be traceable to identified input data, versioned code, relevant configuration and parameters, computational environment, a specific output, and a run identifier or reproducible execution path where appropriate.


Decision documentation — Required
Record consequential decisions in a durable location: exclusion rules, case-definition changes, parameter changes, source substitutions, boundary changes, modeling assumptions, workflow redesigns, and release decisions. Trivial coding choices do not need formal decision records. Git history, issues, pull requests, or a decision log may satisfy this requirement when the decision, rationale, responsible person, and date are recoverable.


Publication or release — Required at external release
Before external release, complete a clean render or workflow execution; document source data; identify code version; synchronize manuscript, code, figures, and tables; provide data/code availability statements; record licenses or restrictions and known limitations; and complete review proportionate to risk and importance. A separate release package or checklist is required only when the release context warrants it.


Handoff and closeout — Required when responsibility changes, work pauses indefinitely, or the project closes
All active projects must avoid undocumented personal dependencies and keep current README, repository, data-location, known-issue, and reproduction information. An actual handoff record is required when responsibility changes. A final closeout record is required when work pauses indefinitely or the project closes; it records access transfer, archive/retention, unfinished work, removal or transfer of personal dependencies, and the authoritative final version.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
6. Requirements by project type
These are conditionally required when the project class applies.

Spatial and spatiotemporal projects
Record CRS and datum, coordinate units, extent, resolution or spatial support, raster origin/alignment, spatial mask, boundary source/version, spatial transformations, coordinate uncertainty, and sensitive-location handling. For example, a map can be irreproducible when a boundary release or raster alignment is not recorded.


Epidemiological and surveillance projects
Record case definition and version/effective dates, event/report date meanings, denominator, deduplication, linkage, reporting delays, jurisdictional changes, confidentiality restrictions, and snapshot/extraction date. A changed case definition or delayed report can otherwise make two valid-looking estimates incomparable.


Ecological and field-data projects
Record sampling design and locations, taxonomic identifiers, units, detection limits, observer/instrument, effort, missing observations, and sensor calibration where relevant. Field effort and detection limits can change apparent abundance even when the analysis code is unchanged.


Genomics and phylogenetics projects
Record sample identifiers, sample-to-sequence linkage, accessions, reference genome, database versions, read-processing workflow, filters, alignment, tree-building configuration, metadata joins, and sensitive host/location handling. A sequence alignment without its sample linkage and filtering record is not a transferable input.


Statistical, mathematical, and simulation models
Record model purpose, conceptual structure, variables, parameters and units, initial/boundary conditions, calibration data, validation, stochastic seeds, replicate strategy, scenarios, acceptance criteria, and limitations. A simulation result without seed and scenario definitions cannot be checked or extended.


Operational workflows
Record production schedule, input availability, failure behavior, logging, alerting, retry behavior, output validation, responsible operator, and change control. Operational outputs require an owner who can explain what happened when an input is late or invalid.


HPC workflows
Record submission script, software environment, modules/container, resource request, job identifier, array definition, input manifest, output destination, stdout/stderr logs, failure and retry status, and the relationship between local and cluster environments. Use templates/hpc-run-record-template.yml.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
8. Research-lifecycle checkpoints
Each gate is a concise, verifiable checkpoint. A failed gate is recorded and corrected or handled through an exception.

1. Project initiation

Identity, objective, audience, outputs, status, owner, and authoritative location are recorded.
Scope, risks, data restrictions, and likely project type are stated.
README contains the concise scope statement; a standalone charter exists if the project triggers that condition.
Planned data locations and access owners are identified.
Initial environment and workflow approach are recorded.



2. Data intake

Source identifier, provider/collector, acquisition date, original name, version, and restriction are recorded.
Source data are preserved or the reason is documented.
Required metadata and spatial/temporal conventions are available; a separate dictionary exists when warranted.
Source-to-derived plan and checks are identified.
Sensitive or governed data have an approved storage/access decision.



3. Analysis readiness

Inputs, code, configuration, parameters, and environment record are discoverable.
Consequential manual steps and decisions are documented.
QA/QC checks are defined and applicable.
Entry point or execution path is identified.
Expected outputs and completion criteria are stated.



4. Result review

Checks ran and exceptions are recorded.
Reported outputs map to input, code, parameters, environment, and run/output IDs.
Model, simulation, spatial, genomic, or operational diagnostics are reviewed where applicable.
Limitations and unresolved decisions are visible.
A reviewer appropriate to project risk is identified.



5. Publication or operational release

Clean execution or render succeeds.
Code, manuscript, figures, tables, and outputs are synchronized.
Data/code availability, licenses, and access restrictions are stated.
Release review and approval are recorded.
Version, archive, and public/private locations are identified.



6. Handoff when responsibility changes

README and inventory are current.
Access, credentials ownership, and data locations are transferred safely.
Principal-output reproduction steps succeed or limitations are recorded.
Known issues, unfinished work, and next actions are listed.
New responsible roles accept the handoff.



7. Closeout when work pauses indefinitely or ends

Authoritative final version is named.
Archive, retention, and disposal decisions are recorded.
Reproducibility materials and restrictions are preserved.
Undocumented personal dependencies are removed or transferred.
Closeout record and contact for future questions are stored.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
9. Proportionality
Documentation and controls scale with project longevity, contributors, data sensitivity, analytical complexity, computational cost, operational importance, publication and regulatory implications, likelihood of handoff, and cost of reconstruction.







Profile
Proportionate minimum




Small exploratory analysis
README containing the concise scope statement, source-data record, scripts, environment note, result traceability, and no separate charter unless another trigger applies


Publication-oriented research
Full data inventory, dependency record, QA/QC documentation, review, release preparation, archive plan, and a standalone charter because publication intent triggers it


Operational or high-consequence workflow
Formal configuration, logging, validation, failure recovery, review authority, controlled releases, and documented ownership



A standalone charter is conditionally required when a project has multiple contributors or organizations, persists beyond a short exploratory period, has external funding or formal deliverables, publication intent, operational use, sensitive or governed data, substantial computational cost, formal handoff expectations, or consequential policy, regulatory, or management use.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
10. Exceptions
Use templates/project-exception-record.md. An exception must record the unmet requirement, reason, consequence, compensating control, responsible person, approval authority, review date, and closure status. An exception cannot override legal, contractual, security, privacy, or institutional requirements. Approval authority remains an open policy decision.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
11. Review checklist
Use templates/project-readiness-checklist.md at the lifecycle gates. The reviewer should be able to locate the authoritative README, inputs, code, parameters, environment, QA record, output/run inventory, decisions, restrictions, and handoff/closeout state.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
12. Related templates
The Templates listing provides copyable Markdown, CSV, and YAML starting points for the artifacts above. Templates are not approved policy by themselves; adapt them and record meaningful deviations.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard
text:
13. Evidence base
This proposal combines observed GeoEpi practice in the practice audit with external guidance: The Turing Way, Good Enough Practices in Scientific Computing, TIER Protocol, RDMkit, DataONE, FAIR Principles, FAIR Principles for Research Software, CARE Principles, USDA NAL guidance, CDC Field Epidemiology Manual, FGDC metadata, GBIF georeferencing, Ecological Metadata Language, and Ecological Forecasting Initiative. Access/review date: 2026-08-05.



Standard area
Principal external guidance
GeoEpi evidence
Policy interpretation




Project organization and README
Good Enough Practices; The Turing Way
READMEs and recognizable project entry points recur across the sample.
Require discoverable identity and scope, not a fixed folder tree.


Source-data protection and provenance
RDMkit; DataONE
OSF/archive links and project-specific data assets recur; acquisition and transformation records are inconsistent.
Require source protection and provenance information; separate tables are conditional.


Metadata and data dictionaries
DataONE; Ecological Metadata Language
Data dictionaries and workflow notes appear in some mature projects.
Require understandable variables, units, codes, and spatial/temporal meaning.


Version control and scripted analysis
The Turing Way; Good Enough Practices
Versioned R scripts are present throughout the sample.
Require version control or a documented exception; retain consequential transformations.


Computational environments
The Turing Way; RDMkit
Environment records and lockfiles are uneven; EpiPlume exposes detailed computational configuration.
Require proportional environment information, not one package manager.


QA/QC
The Turing Way; Good Enough Practices
EpiPlume exposes tests and validation scripts; other projects expose fewer formal checks.
Require workflow-appropriate checks; scripts and retained reports may satisfy the record.


Result traceability and reproduction packages
TIER Protocol
Rendered supporting-information sites and OSF archives recur, but run/output inventories vary.
Require traceability for reported or operational results; formal packages are event- or risk-dependent.


Collaboration and decision records
The Turing Way
Project ownership, decisions, and handoff information are not consistently visible.
Require durable consequential decisions; Git history/issues may suffice.


FAIR data
FAIR Principles
External archives and publication links support reuse in several projects.
Use FAIR as an orientation, subject to access and governance constraints.


FAIR research software
FAIR Principles for Research Software
Licenses and citation metadata are inconsistent across repositories.
Recommend reusable licensing and citation; institutional policy remains open.


CARE and responsible governance
CARE Principles
Public repository review cannot establish governance for sensitive or Indigenous data.
Require authority, responsibility, and restrictions to be identified without inventing policy.


Spatial metadata and georeferencing
FGDC; GBIF
Spatial rasters, boundaries, and model domains recur; CRS and uncertainty records vary.
Conditionally require CRS, datum, extent, alignment, provenance, and uncertainty.


Epidemiological data management
CDC Field Epidemiology Manual
Surveillance and outbreak repositories expose model/report workflows but not consistently case-data metadata.
Conditionally require case definitions, dates, denominators, linkage, and snapshots.


Ecological metadata and forecasting
EML; EFI
Ecological and simulation workflows are represented, but forecast records are not uniform.
Conditionally require sampling, measurement, effort, calibration, scenario, and forecast metadata.


Publication and preservation
TIER Protocol; DataONE
Publications, rendered reports, and OSF links recur in several repositories.
Require release readiness and preservation decisions at the relevant event.



Evidence informs this proposal but does not itself establish GeoEpi policy. The proposal uses original prose and flags areas requiring institutional interpretation in Open policy decisions.

title: Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard

See Open policy decisions.

title: Plan a Project
text:
Is a separate charter warranted?






Conditionally required



A standalone charter is warranted when the project has multiple contributors or organizations, publication intent, external funding or formal deliverables, operational use, sensitive or governed data, substantial computational expense, long duration, formal handoff expectations, or consequential policy, regulatory, or management use. A small exploratory project may keep purpose, owner, scope, outputs, and status in its README.


The decision itself should be visible. Record “README scope is sufficient” or link the charter; do not create a formal file only to satisfy a checklist.

title: Plan a Project
text:
Initiation gate

Objective, intended output, owner, authoritative location, and status are recorded.
Included and excluded work, dependencies, and assumptions are visible.
Roles and decision authority are assigned.
Project consequence and complexity are classified proportionately.
Anticipated data, restrictions, storage, computing, and external dependencies are identified.
Completion criteria and review authority are stated.
A README or charter contains the required scope information.
Unresolved institutional questions are linked to Open Policy Decisions.

This gate authorizes planning to proceed to data-management planning and acquisition; it does not approve analysis or release.

title: Plan a Project
text:
Evidence and interpretation
The planning workflow draws on the existing resource catalog, especially The Turing Way, Good Enough Practices in Scientific Computing, RDMkit, DataONE, and the TIER Protocol. These sources support explicit project purpose, durable documentation, version control, data-management planning, reproducibility, and handoff. Access date: 2026-08-05. External guidance informs this workflow but does not establish GeoEpi or institutional policy.

title: Research Practices
text:
The Lab Book organizes work around a lifecycle:
plan -> acquire -> organize -> analyze -> validate -> collaborate -> communicate -> preserve
Stages overlap and may repeat. A revised project plan can trigger new acquisition work; an intake discrepancy can require a scope decision. Each page distinguishes the Draft minimum, Conditionally required, Recommended, Stronger practice, Example, and Stop and resolve levels.
This first implementation covers Plan and Acquire. The later stages are not presented as complete guidance.

  analyze --> validate[Validate]

title: Research Practices
text:
Choose a starting point

Starting a new project for a short gateway and initiation checklist.
Plan a project when purpose, scope, roles, outputs, or completion criteria are unsettled.
Plan data management when access, storage, restrictions, identifiers, time, space, or computing need decisions.
Receive a one-time dataset when a file, archive, extract, sequence batch, raster, or field export arrives.
Design recurring or programmatic acquisition for APIs, databases, feeds, portals, and scheduled extracts.
Assess intake acceptance when deciding whether incoming data can enter the Organize stage.

The Lab Book separates draft policy, task guidance, templates, and examples. The Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard supplies the governing draft framework; these pages explain how to satisfy relevant information requirements without prescribing one folder tree, storage platform, workflow engine, or environment.

title: Acquire Data
text: Acquisition is more than downloading or receiving files. It includes authorization, specification, preservation, registration, initial inspection, clarification, and an explicit acceptance decision.

title: Acquire Data
text:
Acquisition workflow

Authorize the source, access, and intended use.
Specify expected files, tables, period, geography, format, and documentation.
Receive or extract into an approved intake location.
Preserve the delivered representation before correction or transformation.
Register project context, source, and snapshot identifiers; add a separate intake ID when the delivery pattern or consequence warrants it.
Validate enough to assess completeness and plausibility.
Clarify discrepancies with the provider or data owner.
Accept or reject for staging and further organization using an explicit status.

title: Acquire Data
text:
Choose the acquisition type



Type
Start here




One-time file, archive, sequence batch, raster, or field export
Data intake


Public download or collaborator delivery
Data intake


API, database extraction, recurring feed, or scheduled download
Recurring and programmatic data


Sensor or laboratory stream
Data intake, then adapt the recurring-data guidance



Use the data-source inventory, data dictionary, data-intake record, and file manifest as needed. The project readiness checklist records the gate without requiring a separate file for every item.






Proposed minimum requirement



The Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard requires source protection, provenance, restrictions, metadata, and result traceability. Receiving a file is not the same as accepting a dataset for staging. Intake acceptance does not establish analytical validity, model suitability, publication readiness, or authorization for every downstream use. Acceptance only determines whether the delivery may enter staging and further organization.

title: Acquire Data
text:
Evidence and interpretation
The workflow draws on the existing resource catalog, especially RDMkit, DataONE, the FAIR Principles, CARE Principles, USDA NAL, CDC, FGDC, GBIF, EML, and EFI guidance. These sources support source preservation, provenance, metadata, access and governance, spatial documentation, epidemiological extraction context, ecological documentation, and versioned recurring data. Access date: 2026-08-05. External guidance informs this workflow but does not establish GeoEpi or institutional policy.

title: GeoEpi Lab Book
text:
Draft guidance



The Lab Book is a living resource. Draft pages and proposed policy require review; they do not establish approved laboratory policy.
Welcome to the GeoEpi Lab Book, a shared place for practices that help geographical epidemiology remain understandable, defensible, reproducible, and transferable across people, projects, and time.

title: GeoEpi Lab Book
text:
Find your next step

Start a project for a minimum setup and scope.
Assess project readiness at lifecycle checkpoints.
Document incoming data with a source inventory.
Find a template for reusable project records.
Prepare a handoff before responsibility changes.
Review the minimum standard for the proposed baseline.
Research Practices for the lifecycle from planning through preservation.
Domain Guidance for spatial, epidemiological, ecological, genomic, and modeling topics.
Lab Standards for future lab-level decisions.
Templates for reusable project and documentation structures.
Resources for an annotated external catalog.

The intended outcome is that a lab member can join a project, understand what was done and why, reproduce an important result where access permits, identify uncertainty, and continue the work without relying on undocumented memory.

title: Purpose of the Lab Book
text: Geographical epidemiology joins data, place, time, biology, and models. Small undocumented choices can change an analysis, while staff changes and long timelines can make a sound result difficult to recover.

title: Purpose of the Lab Book
text: Geographical epidemiology joins data, place, time, biology, and models. Small undocumented choices can change an analysis, while staff changes and long timelines can make a sound result difficult to recover.

title: Purpose of the Lab Book
text:
What this site is for
The Lab Book collects concise, reviewable guidance for planning, acquiring, organizing, analyzing, validating, collaborating, communicating, and preserving research. It points to templates and external resources without replacing primary methods papers, data-use agreements, or formal institutional policies. The Lab Book remains distinct from the GeoEpi organization website and GitHub organization.

title: Purpose of the Lab Book
text:
What this site is not
This is not a complete textbook, a substitute for scientific judgment, or an approved policy register. Requirements will be labeled and approved explicitly; until then, content is draft guidance.

title: Contributing
text:
See CONTRIBUTING.md for the repository workflow. Propose changes on a branch, preserve metadata, write in your own words, cite the evidence or source basis, and request review when a change could affect a lab requirement.






Warning



Until governance is finalized, a pull request can improve draft text but cannot by itself turn it into an approved lab requirement.

title: How to Use This Site
text:
Start with Start Here, then use the lifecycle pages in Research Practices and the domain index when a project has specialized needs.






Read the labels



Required, Recommended, and Optional describe the intended strength of a practice. Draft guidance signals material that has not been approved as lab policy. Example demonstrates a pattern without imposing it.


Pages include review metadata near the top. Use the repository actions to view or edit source, or report a problem. A page’s owner coordinates review; it is not automatically the sole author.

title: Domain Guidance
text:
Future guidance will connect general research practices to the risks and conventions of spatial, epidemiological, ecological, genomic, and modeling work. Potential topics include coordinate reference systems, geocoding, case definitions, sampling and detection, genomic provenance, model checking, uncertainty, and responsible communication.
Domain pages should be developed with subject-matter review and should not be inferred from the resource catalog alone.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Proposed minimum requirement



The Minimum GeoEpi Project Standard requires source protection, provenance, restrictions, metadata, and traceability. Preserve the received source package and record enough evidence to identify, inspect, restrict, and accept or reject it for staging. Intake acceptance does not establish analytical validity, model suitability, publication readiness, or authorization for every downstream use.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Definitions for intake

Source: the provider’s conceptual dataset or data system.
Snapshot: a specific received, downloaded, extracted, or released representation of the source.
Intake event: the documented act of receiving or extracting a snapshot.
Preserved source package: the retained original delivered representation before local correction or normalization.
Staged data: a controlled working representation prepared from the preserved source package.
Derived data: data created through documented transformation.
Authoritative location: the location designated as current for a specified artifact; it is not necessarily the provider’s original system.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Before receipt
Record or confirm the provider, data owner, access authorization, expected dataset, expected files or tables, format, delivery method, version or time period, geographic and temporal support, restrictions, identifiers, expected documentation, and contact for discrepancies.
Do not accept credentials in README files, Git, templates, or logs.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Receive into an approved location
Place incoming data first in an approved source or intake location. The location should prevent accidental overwrite, preserve original names where useful, preserve the delivered package, limit access appropriately, and separate received material from transformed data. No universal folder name or storage platform is required.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Assign identifiers
Every received dataset must have project identity or authoritative project context, a source ID, and a snapshot, release, extraction, or acquisition ID sufficient to distinguish the received version. A separate intake ID is Conditionally required when more than one delivery or extraction may occur, replacement or corrected deliveries are possible, multiple people or systems handle intake, a formal manifest or audit trail is needed, or the workflow is recurring, regulated, operational, or high consequence. For a simple one-time delivery, the snapshot or acquisition ID may also serve as the intake ID.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Preserve the source package
Retain the original delivered representation where lawful and practical: a downloaded archive, spreadsheet, database extract, API response, sequence files, field-data export, and associated documentation. Do not silently edit the preserved source copy. Corrections and normalization belong in staged or derived representations.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Record provenance
At minimum, record source, provider or collector, acquisition method, acquisition date/time where relevant, source identifier, version or release, original filename or table, local authoritative location, restriction or license, access contact, related agreement or documentation, transformation-record location, and a checksum when proportionate. Use the existing data-source inventory rather than creating redundant records.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
File or object manifest
Use a file-level manifest for a multi-file delivery, archive, repeated snapshot, sequence batch, raster stack, model-input bundle, transfer across systems, or regulated/high-consequence workflow. A checksum is Conditionally required when integrity across transfers, storage systems, releases, or repeated processing materially matters. It is not required for every trivial temporary file.
Use the data-file manifest template.
In that manifest, relative_path is relative to the documented intake or preserved-source root. source_modified_time is the provider’s or source system’s time, not local receipt time, and should include a time zone or an explicit source convention. Checksum fields may be blank when integrity checking is not proportionate. supersedes should reference a stable file, snapshot, or manifest ID. Use the documented intake statuses in validation_status: received, pending validation, pending clarification, accepted for staging, accepted with documented limitation, rejected, or superseded; the row marked as an example must be deleted before use.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Initial content inspection
Check only enough to decide whether the delivery is plausible and ready for further organization: identifiers, key variables, units, missing-value conventions, interpretable dates and geography, expected categories, consistent confidentiality markings, and absence of obvious truncation or corruption. Intake inspection is not final analytical QA/QC.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Resolve discrepancies
Record the discrepancy, date identified, source contacted, clarification received, replacement delivery, affected files, and acceptance decision. Never silently substitute or overwrite a corrected delivery. Link related deliveries through snapshot or intake identifiers.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Status-transition model





flowchart TD
  received[received] --> pending_validation[pending validation]
  pending_validation --> pending_clarification[pending clarification, when needed]
  pending_validation --> accepted_staging[accepted for staging]
  pending_clarification --> accepted_staging
  pending_validation --> rejected[rejected]
  pending_clarification --> rejected
  accepted_staging --> limited[accepted with documented limitation]
  accepted_staging --> superseded[superseded later]
  limited --> superseded






superseded does not delete or overwrite the earlier intake record. Rejection does not necessarily mean that the source is scientifically invalid; it means that this delivery must not enter staging. A pending delivery must not silently enter downstream analysis. An accepted-with-limitation decision must record the limitation, likely consequence, downstream restriction, responsible decision-maker, and required follow-up.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Acceptance statuses
Use only these statuses for this intake workflow: received means material has arrived but has not been inspected; pending validation means technical or content inspection is incomplete; pending clarification means a material question has been sent to the provider or owner; accepted for staging means the delivery may enter the Organize stage; accepted with documented limitation means it may enter staging with a visible limitation and responsible decision-maker; rejected means it must not enter staging; and superseded means a later identified delivery replaces it while the original record remains preserved. These labels guide the workflow and do not establish institutional classification terminology.






Stop and resolve



Pause intake or analysis when authorization is missing or unclear; unexpected PII or protected information is present; restrictions conflict with the planned workflow; the source or version cannot be identified; required files are absent; corruption is suspected; identifiers cannot be reconciled; temporal fields are ambiguous; CRS or spatial support cannot be determined; the delivery differs materially from its description; replacement files overwrite prior evidence; or the intended storage location is not approved.
These conditions require clarification, not improvised assumptions.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Domain-specific intake checks

Spatial data
Record CRS, datum, units, extent, resolution, grid origin/alignment, masks, boundary version, and NoData convention.


Epidemiological and surveillance data
Record case-definition version, event/report/extract dates, denominator, deduplication, jurisdiction, reporting delay, and confidentiality.


Ecological and field data
Record sampling effort, collector, instrument, calibration, taxonomic identifiers, detection limits, and field revisions.


Genomics and phylogenetics
Record sample-to-sequence linkage, accession, reference genome, database release, read-processing status, and metadata restrictions.


Model and simulation inputs
Record parameter version, units, scenario, initial conditions, boundary conditions, and calibration source.

title: Data Intake and Acceptance
text:
Intake completion gate

Authorization, owner, provider, restrictions, and access contact are recorded.
Project context, source ID, and snapshot/release/extraction/acquisition ID are assigned.
A separate intake ID is assigned when the delivery pattern or consequence makes it conditionally required; a simple one-time delivery may reuse its snapshot ID.
The delivered source package is preserved at an authoritative location.
Expected and received contents are compared.
Technical and initial content inspections are recorded.
Required metadata, identifiers, units, dates, geography, and domain fields are interpretable.
Discrepancies and clarifications are linked to the affected delivery.
Acceptance status and responsible decision-maker are recorded.
The data are explicitly received, pending validation, pending clarification, accepted for staging, accepted with documented limitation, rejected, or superseded.

Passing this gate allows an accepted delivery to enter the Organize stage. It does not certify analytical validity, model suitability, publication readiness, or authorization for every downstream use.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text: Recurring acquisition includes APIs, databases, portals, scheduled extracts, surveillance feeds, sensor feeds, automated downloads, and revised historical datasets. Do not implement a client or download script here; record what a reproducible retrieval must preserve.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text:
Record the request specification
Retain the endpoint or database, dataset/table, query, request parameters, date range, geography, variables, filters, pagination behavior, extraction timestamp, API/database version where available, code version, and configuration version. Do not store secrets in configuration committed to Git.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text:
Preserve snapshots
When a retrieval can change, produce a preserved snapshot or immutable release record appropriate to the project. Distinguish the live source, retrieved snapshot, normalized data, and current analytical dataset. A live URL is not a reproducibility identifier.
Each accepted retrieval should produce or update a source inventory record, snapshot or retrieval ID, intake or acceptance status, schema/revision assessment, and a preserved snapshot when the source can change or the workflow consequence warrants it. A retrieval manifest is Conditionally required for multi-file, repeated, transferred, regulated, operational, or integrity-sensitive retrievals.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text:
Revisions and late-arriving data
Document replacement behavior, backfills, corrected records, reporting delays, revised historical periods, schema changes, changed geographic boundaries, and changed case definitions. “Latest” is not an adequate identifier for a reproducible retrieval.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text:
Idempotence and overwrite safety
Recommended: design retrievals that do not silently overwrite prior snapshots, detect existing valid outputs, record partial failure, support safe retry, and distinguish completed, failed, incomplete, and superseded retrievals.






Stronger practice



For a consequential recurring workflow, retain an immutable retrieval manifest and an automated completeness check for every snapshot. This strengthens traceability without making a scheduler, workflow engine, or container universally required.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text:
Pagination and completeness
Before accepting a retrieval, retain evidence that all pages or partitions were retrieved, expected date or spatial coverage is present, rate limiting did not silently truncate results, retries did not duplicate records, and response counts are plausible.
A successful HTTP response, database connection, or completed download command is not evidence of complete retrieval.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text:
Schema drift
Check for added or removed variables, type changes, category changes, renamed fields, changed missing-value conventions, altered units, and changed coordinate definitions. Record how a change was handled; do not silently coerce a new schema into an old one.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text:
Retrieval manifest
Recommended, conditionally required for consequential recurring workflows: retain a manifest containing retrieval ID, source ID, snapshot ID, intake or acceptance status, requested period, request hash where useful, retrieved files, status, timestamps, software/configuration version, checksums where proportionate, log location, schema/revision assessment, and error or retry information.






Example



A weekly environmental raster retrieval should record the requested weeks, geographic tiles, CRS, grid alignment, response status, and snapshot identifier. A recurring surveillance extract should also record the query, case-definition version, report-date window, late-report behavior, and database snapshot or extraction timestamp.

title: Recurring and Programmatic Data
text:
Acceptance gate for recurring data

Request specification and source identifier are versioned.
Retrieval timestamp, requested period, geography, and configuration are recorded.
A snapshot or immutable release record exists when the source can change.
Pagination, partition, coverage, and response-count checks are recorded.
Schema drift and revision behavior are assessed.
Retry, failure, duplicate, incomplete, and superseded states are distinguishable.
Credentials are kept outside committed code, configuration, logs, and templates.
The resulting snapshot is registered through the data-source inventory and, when useful, the file manifest.
The retrieval has an intake or acceptance status, schema/revision assessment, and preserved snapshot when required.

title: Plan Data Management
text: Data-management planning is a set of decisions that must be recorded, not necessarily a separate formal document. Reconcile anticipated information with the actual data-source inventory during intake.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Anticipated data inventory
Before acquisition, record the source or provider, expected format, approximate volume, delivery frequency, temporal and spatial support, identifiers, update behavior, access conditions, likely sensitivity, and expected authoritative location.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Access and governance
Identify the data owner, access contact, authorized users, data-use agreement, redistribution and publication restrictions, expiration or destruction requirements, sensitive locations, PII or linked identifiers, and Indigenous or community governance considerations where applicable.






Stop and resolve



Do not invent institutional classifications or assume that a storage platform is approved for every data class. Link unresolved questions about classification, storage, cloud services, backups, retention, PII, sensitive spatial data, and public repositories to Open Policy Decisions.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Storage and authoritative copies
Distinguish the delivery location, preserved source copy, active working storage, derived-data storage, repository code and documentation, temporary computation, output storage, and archive or release location. GitHub is not the default location for large, restricted, or non-redistributable source data.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Backup and recovery planning
Record the authoritative copy, backup responsibility, expected recovery path, consequences of loss, whether restoration has been tested, and whether the data can be reacquired. Do not invent a backup frequency; use the applicable institutional or agreement-based requirement.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Identifiers and naming
Plan stable identifiers for the project, source dataset, source snapshot or release, derived dataset, model scenario, run, and output. Prefer identifiers that remain stable when filenames change. Do not prescribe one universal naming convention.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Temporal conventions
Plan for event date, report date, extraction date, acquisition date, processing date, time zone, daylight-saving behavior, epidemiological week convention, and revision or late-reporting behavior.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Spatial conventions
Plan for CRS and datum, units, geographic extent, spatial support, resolution, raster alignment, boundary source/version, and sensitive-coordinate handling.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Computational planning
Anticipate the software stack, packages, GIS software, databases, command-line tools, containers, HPC, storage volume, memory, runtime, parallel execution, external services, and credentials. Dependency locking and containers are proportional practices, not universal requirements. Never place credentials in Git, README files, templates, or logs.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Release and preservation planning
At initiation, identify likely publication repository, code release, data release or access statement, persistent identifier, archive, retention owner, and closeout trigger. Not all data must be made public; access restrictions and agreements control.

title: Plan Data Management
text:
Planning gate

Purpose and scope are recorded.
Responsible roles and decision authority are known.
Anticipated sources and restrictions are identified.
Authoritative locations and recovery responsibilities are planned.
Computing and external dependencies are plausible.
Expected outputs and acceptance criteria are stated.
Unresolved policy questions are visible.
A proportional README or charter exists.

Passing this gate means that data-management conditions are planned well enough to begin authorized acquisition. It does not accept any received dataset.

title: Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
text: State whether the project addresses a scientific question, operational objective, decision-support need, software or infrastructure objective, or training/demonstration purpose. “Build a model” and “analyze the data” describe techniques, not what the work is meant to accomplish.

title: Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
text: State whether the project addresses a scientific question, operational objective, decision-support need, software or infrastructure objective, or training/demonstration purpose. “Build a model” and “analyze the data” describe techniques, not what the work is meant to accomplish.

title: Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
section: Define the analytical or operational unit
text:
Define the analytical or operational unit
Record the population or system, geography, time period, outcome or response, unit of observation, unit of inference, intended comparison, intended users, and decision or publication context.






Example



A county-week disease model may use individual case records as inputs but make inference about county-week incidence. The scope should name both units so that data receipt, denominators, and completion criteria are not confused.

title: Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
text:
Set explicit boundaries
Document included work, excluded work, known dependencies, assumptions, unavailable data, activities deferred to later phases, and the scope-change process. Exclusions define the project as much as inclusions.

title: Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
text:
Define outputs
Distinguish internal analytical outputs, manuscript figures and tables, reusable datasets, software releases, operational products, dashboards, forecasts, reports, and archival packages. Every consequential output needs an authoritative location and responsible owner.






Example



A weekly raster workflow may be complete only when the expected dates and spatial coverage are present. “The script ran” is not the same completion criterion as “the weekly product is available for every planned region and week.”

title: Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
text:
Define completion and acceptance
Before methods are selected, record what counts as complete, which checks must pass, who reviews the result, what limitations are acceptable, and what would prevent release or operational use. Keep these as planned acceptance criteria; detailed analytical validation belongs to a later lifecycle stage.

title: Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
text:
Determine the project profile








Profile
Planning depth
Review, environment, and handoff expectation




Small exploratory project
README scope, likely sources, outputs, and immediate risks
Lightweight environment note, proportionate review, and visible next action


Publication-oriented collaborative project
Charter or equivalent scope, contributors, data restrictions, outputs, and acceptance criteria
Recorded review, reproducible environment, source/data controls, and planned archive/handoff


Operational or high-consequence project
Formal ownership, dependencies, failure consequences, controlled outputs, and change authority
Explicit environment, review authority, operational owner, recovery path, and handoff preparation

title: Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
text:
Record consequential decisions
Use the lightest durable record that preserves the decision, rationale, responsible person, and date. A README history, GitHub issue, project note, decision log, or formal exception record may be sufficient. Do not require a formal decision record for routine coding choices.

title: Define Project Scope and Responsibilities
text:
GeoEpi examples






Example



A phylogenetic project may define its deliverable as a reviewed tree plus a sample-to-sequence metadata table. Without that linkage, a visually complete tree may not meet the project’s acceptance criteria.


The project charter template is Conditionally required when project consequence or coordination warrants it. The README template supports small projects. The readiness checklist supports the initiation review.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Internal draft



This is an informational practice audit, not a quality score, ranking, or assessment of scientific correctness. It records observable repository and website practices and requires human review.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Review boundary
The audit reviewed the GeoEpi organization profile, the public organization website repository, the organization .github repository, the public Notebook repository, and eight purposively selected research repositories. The review date was 2026-08-05. The machine-readable observations are in standards/data/geoepi-repository-audit.csv.
The review examined public repository trees, READMEs, key workflow and documentation files, GitHub workflow directories, repository license metadata and license files, citation files or references, test paths, and plausible entry points. No code was executed and no scientific validation or compliance review was performed. A yes means that an artifact was visible and usable enough for this limited review; partial, unclear, and no do not imply that a practice is absent from private archives, external services, or project knowledge.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Organization references
The GeoEpi organization profile describes work on animal disease transmission and outbreak dynamics and links the group website and research notebook. The profile describes the Notebook as a living resource for reproducible science in scientific computing, coding, data management, and modeling, and explicitly says it is not a compendium of rigid requirements. The organization .github profile repeats this scope and points to OSF for project management, storage, version control, and archival support.
The organization website was reviewed for navigation, typography, neutral colors, logo/favicon assets, and the distinction between a research-group homepage and an operational notebook. Its research scope spans statistical and mathematical modeling, bioinformatics, artificial intelligence, and molecular-to-landscape scales. These observations inform limited visual continuity; they do not authorize copying the website structure or branding wholesale.

text:

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Workflow types represented
The sample covers spatial and spatiotemporal analysis, outbreak and surveillance analysis, ecological or field-adjacent data, genomics and phylogenetics, mathematical and simulation models, rendered supporting-information sites, interactive applications, and high-performance computing. That diversity supports a project standard based on traceability and handoff rather than a single folder tree or software stack.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Recurring documentation gaps
The sample showed inconsistent or hard-to-find records for software environments, data classification and restrictions, source-to-derived transformations, checksums or acquisition dates, output/run inventories, decision history, tests and CI, citation metadata, licenses, and closeout/handoff status. Several repositories contain useful rendered products but do not make the authoritative source, current execution path, or reproducibility boundary obvious from the top-level README.
These are aggregate observations from a limited public snapshot. A gap means that the item was not readily discoverable during this review; it does not mean that project members have not documented it elsewhere. This page is provisional, is based only on public repository contents, is not a compliance review, and is not a ranking.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Practices mature enough to standardize
The following are sufficiently cross-cutting to propose as minimum requirements: project identity and ownership; a current README; documented separation of source, staged, derived, code, configuration, documentation, outputs, logs, and temporary material; source-data protection; data provenance; data classification; data dictionaries; retained scripted transformations; version control with explicit exclusions; proportional environment records; explicit consequential parameters; quality checks appropriate to the workflow; result traceability; durable decision records; release readiness; and handoff/closeout records.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Recommended rather than universal
The following should remain recommended or conditional: one universal directory tree; renv for every R project; containers; continuous integration; unit-test coverage; workflow orchestration; formal metadata standards such as EML; checksums for every file; public release of data; notebooks as the primary execution format; OSF or any one storage provider; and a specific HPC scheduler. They become conditionally required when project sensitivity, scale, operational consequence, computational cost, publication commitments, or handoff risk makes them necessary.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Repository-specific patterns not generalized
Targets and Slurm manifest ledgers in EpiPlume, BEAST XML and cluster scripts in phylo-tutorial, Shiny delivery in seir-vector, and publication-oriented rendered sites in several repositories are valuable patterns but are not universal minimums. A repository may use Quarto, R Markdown, a workflow engine, a scheduler, a database, a notebook, or a scripted command-line entry point when the chosen path is documented and traceable.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Discrepancies and unresolved interpretation
Repositories differ in default branch name, whether rendered output is committed, where data are stored, whether a project is a tutorial or publication package, and whether an external archive is part of the authoritative workflow. Public repositories also expose only a subset of access-controlled data and institutional records. Human review is needed to decide institutional terminology for data classification, approved storage and retention, release review, licensing, authorship, and exception authority. These decisions are collected in Open policy decisions.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
External guidance used for comparison
The external comparison used the existing resource catalog, with access dates recorded there and here. The Turing Way emphasizes reproducible research, version control, data management, documentation, testing, review, and collaboration as connected practices. Good Enough Practices in Scientific Computing provides a deliberately pragmatic baseline for research computing. TIER Protocol 4.0 provides a replication-documentation model, while RDMkit organizes FAIR-oriented data management by lifecycle, role, domain, task, and tools.
The FAIR Principles and FAIR Principles for Research Software support findability, accessibility, interoperability, reuse, software quality, and citation. The CARE Principles add collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility, and ethics for Indigenous data. Government and domain-specific comparison points include USDA NAL data-management guidance, the CDC Field Epidemiology Manual, FGDC metadata guidance, GBIF georeferencing best practices, Ecological Metadata Language, and Ecological Forecasting Initiative standards.
These sources are guidance, standards, or community practices—not institutional policy. Where they conflict with USDA, laboratory, information-security, records-management, contractual, privacy, or data-governance requirements, the authoritative requirement controls and the project records the constraint.

title: GeoEpi Practice Audit
text:
Limitations
This is a point-in-time review of public repository material, not an audit of access-controlled archives, computational execution, scientific validity, or compliance. The CSV is intentionally descriptive and must not be used to score or rank repositories.

title: Open Policy Decisions
text:
Human approval required



This page records open decisions. It does not establish institutional policy or authorize a storage system, classification scheme, retention period, release process, or use of generative AI.
The owner, evidence, status, and review point below are role-based placeholders. No named individuals are assigned.

title: Open Policy Decisions
text:
Interim treatment
Record applicable restrictions without inventing official labels. Use the approved system named by the data owner or agreement. Do not upload restricted data, PII, credentials, unpublished confidential material, or protected research content to an unapproved service. Preserve upstream license terms and record uncertainty. Legal, privacy, security, contractual, and institutional requirements cannot be waived by a project exception.
Until approved, each item should receive an evidence-backed decision, decision date, and review date. The proposed standard should then be revised rather than silently converting assumptions into policy.

title: Starting a New Project
text: Write a README with the objective, intended output, owner, authoritative location, current status, likely data sources, and immediate restrictions. Record the next decision, the person who can make it, and whether a separate charter is warranted. Do not start analysis while ownership, source identity, restrictions, or intended outputs remain materially unclear.

title: Starting a New Project
text:
Choose the pathway

Standard project start
Use Plan and Project scope to define purpose, boundaries, outputs, roles, and completion criteria. Then use Data-management planning before receiving data.


Higher-consequence project
Use the same sequence with a standalone project charter, explicit review authority, data-management decisions, environment planning, and a documented handoff expectation. Triggers include publication intent, operational use, sensitive or governed data, substantial computation, formal deliverables, or consequential policy use.


When data arrive
Use Data intake before correcting, renaming, normalizing, or accepting the delivery. Use Recurring and programmatic data for APIs, databases, and scheduled retrievals.

title: Starting a New Project
text:
Compact initiation checklist

Objective, intended output, owner, location, and status are in the README.
Scope boundaries, dependencies, and completion criteria are stated.
Roles, decision authority, data contacts, and restrictions are identified.
Storage, computing, acquisition, and handoff conditions are plausible.
The project uses the readiness checklist at initiation.

title: Guidance Page Authoring Template
text:
Metadata convention
Required front matter: title, description, status, practice-level, audience, domains, topics, owner, last-reviewed, and review-cycle.
Recommended values are draft | proposed | approved | retired | template for status; orientation | minimum | recommended | stronger | example for practice level; and annual | semiannual | event-driven for review cycle. Dates use ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD); tags are lowercase and concise. approved requires an explicit lab review decision.
